events.text: The rains came early and {npc}'s roof gave way over the bed. {He} is sleeping in the kitchen and pretending it is fine.

mem.note: climbed up and fixed my roof

effects.log: Two days on the beams in the rain. {npc} brings you soup on a ladder and complains about the drips you missed.
The carpenter does it in a day. {npc} says it was too expensive and sleeps beautifully.

choices.text: Tell {him} to move in with you

effects.log: {He} refuses, of course. Then {he} stays for a month and rearranges your kitchen.

variants: The early rains brought {npc}'s roof down over the bed. {He} has been sleeping in the kitchen and insisting it is fine.

events.text: A neighbour has been moving the boundary stone between {npc}'s field and the one next door, a hand's width a year, for ten years.

ok.log: The stone goes back. The neighbour watches you carry it and decides on a new hobby.

fail.log: The stone wins, and your back loses. The neighbour waits until you are gone and nudges it forward again.

choices.text: Take it to the village head

mem.note: went to the village head for me

ok.log: The village head walks the boundary with a rope and a long memory. The neighbour pays for the lost rice in winter.

fail.log: The village head walks the boundary with a rope and a long memory, and decides the stone has always been there. Nothing changes.

events.text: {npc} writes: a cousin's wedding is in a month and the family is short of everything: rice wine, a pig, and a respectable relative to sit at the head of the table.

choices.text: Bring the pig and sit at the table

mem.note: came to the wedding with a pig

effects.log: You are the respectable relative. You are asked about your marriage prospects eleven times.

choices.text: Bring the pig and your spouse, and sit at the table

mem.note: came to the wedding with a pig

effects.log: You are the respectable relative. You are asked about your spouse's family, your spouse's health and your spouse's plans eleven times.
The wine is drunk. Your absence is discussed more than the bride.

variants: A letter from {npc}: a cousin is getting married next month, and the family is short of rice wine, a pig, and a relative respectable enough for the head of the table.

events.text: {npc} cannot read, and a letter has come from a government office. {He} has been carrying it around for a week, afraid of what it says.

effects.log: A small tax refund, of all things. {npc} buys a duck with it and invites the whole lane.
It takes a winter of evenings. The first thing {npc} reads alone is your name, which {he} writes on the kitchen wall.

variants: {npc} cannot read, and an official letter has come. {He} has carried it in {his} sleeve for a week, afraid to learn what it says.

events.text: Years ago, {npc} made a vow at a mountain temple to return with an offering if you lived through a childhood fever. {He} is too old now to make the climb.

effects.log: Nine hundred steps. {npc} complains about your posture the whole way and weeps at the top.

choices.text: Go up yourself with the offering

effects.log: The monk says vows kept by children count double. {npc} sleeps soundly for the first time in years.

events.text: A young relative wants to learn martial arts and the family cannot afford a school. {npc} asks, very carefully, whether you would teach.

effects.log: An hour every dawn for a year. The child is terrible, and stubborn, and in ten years better than you were at that age.
The school takes the child. The family tells everyone you paid, which you did not want and secretly enjoy.

variants: A young relative is desperate to learn martial arts, and the family cannot pay for a school. {npc} asks, very carefully, if you might teach.

events.text: {npc}'s youngest has been gambling, and lost a silver hairpin that belonged to a grandmother. The gambling house will sell it on tomorrow.

effects.log: The hairpin comes home. The youngest is made to polish it every week for a year.

choices.text: Talk the owner into giving it back

mem.note: talked the hairpin back out of the house

ok.log: You find the owner's soft spot, which turns out to be an ailing mother. The hairpin comes home, and a bottle of liniment goes the other way.

mem.note: tried to talk the hairpin back

fail.log: The owner finds your soft spot instead, which is your purse. You pay ten taels for the privilege of being refused.

variants: {npc}'s youngest has gambled away a silver hairpin that was a grandmother's. The gambling house sells it on tomorrow.

events.text: {npc} swears the old storehouse is haunted: the rice goes missing at night and something scratches at the door.

choices.text: Sit up all night in the storehouse

ok.log: The ghost is a fox with a litter in the rafters. You come home at dawn with straw in your hair and a story.

mem.note: sat up all night for nothing

fail.log: You see nothing, hear everything, and come home at dawn stiff and cold. The rice goes missing again the next night.

effects.log: The rice keeps going missing. {npc} hangs a charm on the door and does not mention it to you again.

variants: {npc} is certain the old storehouse is haunted. Rice disappears at night, and something scratches at the door.

events.text: A bundle arrives from {npc}: dried persimmons, a pair of thick socks, and a letter that says, in its whole length, 'Eat properly. You {debt}.'

effects.log: {npc} reads your letter to the whole lane, twice, skipping the parts about danger.
You arrive unannounced. {npc} scolds you for not writing first and cooks for three days.

variants: A parcel from {npc}: a string of dried persimmons, two pairs of woollen socks, and a letter of exactly one line. 'Eat properly. You {debt}.'
Inside the bundle from {npc}: socks, dried fruit, and a note that does not waste a single brushstroke. 'Eat properly. You {debt}.'

events.text: {npc} gives you a sword wrapped in oilcloth: your grandfather's, kept under the floor through two famines. 'You {debt}. It should be used.'

effects.log: The blade is old and plain and balanced like nothing you have held. Inside the hilt, a slip of paper: a breathing method in a careful hand.

choices.text: Leave it on the family altar

effects.log: {npc} cries a little, which {he} denies, and polishes the sword every new year.

variants: {npc} unwraps a long oilcloth bundle: your grandfather's sword, hidden under the floorboards through two famines. 'You {debt}. It should be used.'

events.text: {npc} finally writes down the family's medicine recipe for you, the one passed mouth to mouth for five generations. 'Because you {debt}.'

effects.log: It cures exactly one thing: a winter cough. It cures it perfectly.

choices.text: Sell it to a medicine hall

effects.log: The hall pays well. {npc} finds out, as families do. Dinner is very quiet that year.

variants: At last {npc} writes it down for you: the family's medicine recipe, never before put on paper in five generations. 'Because you {debt}.'

events.text: {npc} has, without asking you, found someone suitable. 'You {debt}. Now let me do something for you.' The someone is waiting in the next room.

effects.log: An afternoon of tea and very careful conversation. Whatever comes of it, {npc} is delighted for a month.
The match, it turns out, also climbed out of a window. You meet in the lane outside and laugh until you cannot stand.

variants: Without a word of warning, {npc} has arranged a meeting. 'You {debt}. So let me do something for you.' Someone suitable is drinking tea in the next room.

events.text: {npc} gives you a string of old coins: one put aside every year since you were born, for the day you would need them. You {debt}, {he} says, but that is not why.

effects.log: You never spend them. They are worth almost nothing and you would not sell them for a sect.
A good dinner, a new coat, an afternoon at the theatre. {npc} scolds you for the waste and wears the coat to bed.

variants: {npc} hands you a string of old coins, one saved every year since you were born, for the day you would need them. You {debt}, {he} says, but that is not the reason.

events.text: {npc} sews a protective charm into the lining of your robe while you sleep. You find it a week later, in the middle of a fight, when a blade that should have found you does not.

effects.log: You never take that robe off in a fight again. Superstition, you say. You do not say it to {npc}.

mem.note: came home to say thank you

effects.log: {npc} says the charm did nothing and you were simply lucky. {He} sews another into your other robe.

variants: While you sleep, {npc} stitches a folded charm into the hem of your robe. You do not know it is there until a week later, when a strike that should have landed slides past you as if pushed.
You find the charm only after the fight: a scrap of red paper sewn into your robe by {npc}, right over the place a blade turned aside that afternoon.
